summary: Teaches pupils to apply Pythagoras' Theorem (a²+b²=c²) to find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, including on a coordinate grid. The load-bearing move is identifying the hypotenuse by POSITION (opposite the right angle, always the longest side) — not by its digits — and then letting whether the hypotenuse is known or unknown decide square-and-ADD (finding the hypotenuse) vs square-and-SUBTRACT, hypotenuse²−leg² (finding a shorter side). Experts see one step; novices experience many: identify the hypotenuse, decide whether Pythagoras applies, recall the relationship, choose add vs subtract, substitute, and take the square root.
misconceptions: Assumes the unknown side is always the hypotenuse, so always squares and ADDS — even when asked for a shorter side (the most common error; often triggered by triangle orientation)
Muddles a hypotenuse with a leg — judges by the number rather than by which side is opposite the right angle
When finding a shorter side, subtracts the wrong way around (leg² − hypotenuse² instead of hypotenuse² − leg²)
Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value (e.g. 25 instead of 5)
For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (3+4=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem

activities.title: Pour the squares: seeing a²+b²=c²
steps: Drag the two legs of a right-angled triangle and watch a square inflate on each of the three sides.
Watch the two smaller squares dissolve and tile, piece by piece, into the big square on the longest side, filling it exactly.
Read a live readout that updates to show a²+b²=c² as the legs change.
Optionally tap each square to reveal its area and confirm the two smaller areas sum to the largest.
activities.insight: The theorem is a relationship between the areas of the squares on the three sides: the two smaller squares together exactly fill the square on the hypotenuse, so a²+b² IS c² rather than a formula to memorise.

activities.title: Circle the hypotenuse first, then choose add or subtract
steps: On right-angled triangles drawn in varied orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left), tap or circle the hypotenuse — accepted only when it is the side opposite the right angle, not the longest-looking one on the page.
For each triangle, state whether the hypotenuse is the KNOWN side or the UNKNOWN side before choosing an operation.
Choose square-and-ADD when the unknown side is the hypotenuse; choose square-and-SUBTRACT (hypotenuse²−leg²) when the unknown is a shorter side.
Compare two side-by-side triangles where the same numeric length (e.g. 10) is a leg in one and the hypotenuse in the other, and label each correctly.
Finish each calculation by taking the square root, then check the hypotenuse is the longest side.
activities.insight: A side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle (and so the longest), not because of its digits; which side is unknown — not the size of the numbers — decides whether you add or subtract.

activities.title: Distance between two points as a hypotenuse
steps: Plot two points on a coordinate grid (e.g. (1,2) and (5,5)).
Draw the horizontal and vertical legs between the points explicitly, so the connecting segment is seen as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
Find the horizontal difference (Δx) and vertical difference (Δy), then compute distance = √(Δx²+Δy²).
Try a second pair of points unprompted, constructing the right triangle yourself before calculating.
activities.insight: Finding the straight-line distance between two points is a Pythagoras problem: the segment between them is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical differences.

checkQuestion: Give the pupil three right-angled triangles drawn in DIFFERENT orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left) plus a coordinate grid, and set four tasks to WATCH them do — do not explain first: (1) On each triangle, circle the hypotenuse. (2) Triangle A has the two shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm — find the third side. (3) Triangle B has hypotenuse 13 cm and one shorter side 5 cm — find the other shorter side. (4) Plot the points (1,2) and (5,5) and find the straight-line distance between them. Watch how they identify the hypotenuse, whether they add or subtract, and whether they finish with a square root.
checkAnswer: (1) The hypotenuse is circled as the side opposite the right angle on every triangle, regardless of orientation. (2) √(6²+8²)=√100=10 cm (square and add — finding the hypotenuse). (3) √(13²−5²)=√144=12 cm (square and subtract — finding a shorter side, hypotenuse² minus leg²). (4) Horizontal leg 4, vertical leg 3, distance √(4²+3²)=√25=5 (forms a right triangle from the coordinate differences).
